facts.statement: The genus of this extinct animal is Eremopezus.
facts.quote: genus: Eremopezus

facts.statement: The only known species within the genus is Eremopezus eocaenus.
facts.quote: species: eocaenus

facts.statement: The genus was described by C. W. Andrews in 1904.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Andrews, 1904

facts.statement: Fossils of Eremopezus date to the Late Eocene epoch.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Eocene

facts.statement: Eremopezus eocaenus was a huge bird that was likely flightless.
facts.quote: huge and presumably flightless Eremopezus eocaenus

facts.statement: The fossils were found in rocks deposited between approximately 36 and 33 million years ago.
facts.quote: The rocks its fossils occur in were deposited in the Priabonian, with the oldest dating back to about 36 million years ago (Ma) and the youngest not less than about 33 Ma

facts.statement: The fossils were discovered in the Upper Eocene Jebel Qatrani Formation near Faiyum, Egypt.
facts.quote: Upper Eocene Jebel Qatrani Formation deposits around the Qasr el Sagha escarpment, north of the Birket Qarun lake near Faiyum in Egypt

facts.statement: The original description was based on a distal left tibiotarsus specimen.
facts.quote: It was originally described from a distal left tibiotarsus piece (specimen BMNH A843)

facts.statement: Researchers initially believed Eremopezus was a ratite closely related to the elephant birds of Madagascar.
facts.quote: Eremopezus was initially believed a ratite and loosely allied with the elephant birds of Madagascar

facts.statement: The presence of deep ligamental pits on the distal condyles distinguishes Eremopezus from elephant birds.
facts.quote: The Eremopezus specimen on the other hand has deep ligamental pits on the lateral and medial sides of the distal condyles, which are not found in the elephant birds proper

facts.statement: The tarsometatarsus of Eremopezus resembles that of general ratites like emus or ostriches rather than elephant birds.
facts.quote: The tarsometatarsus is also more similar to that of an unspecific ratite, such as an emu, ostrich or rhea, rather than to the apomorphic one of the elephant birds

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding whether certain fossil eggshells from the Maghreb belong to Eremopezus or to ostriches.
facts.quote: Some fossil eggshells from the Maghreb, described as Psammornis and resembling those of ratite eggs, were assigned to Eremopezus by various authors

facts.statement: The genus name Eremopezus translates to 'walking hermit,' derived from Greek words for a solitary place and walking.
facts.quote: Eremos (ἐρῆμος) is an Ancient Greek term signifying a lonely or solitary place or person: a hermit, a desert or a wasteland

facts.statement: Eremopezus had widely divergent toes capable of flexing through a wide range of positions and strong tendons that provided a firm grip.
facts.quote: its toes were widely divergent and could flex through a wide range of positions, while strong tendons gave the bird a firm grip.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Eremopezus behaved similarly to secretarybirds and shoebills in the swamps of the Jebel Qatrani Formation.
facts.quote: this suggests that Eremopezus behaved similarly in the swamps of the Jebel Qatrani Formation.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Eremopezus represents a separate example of ratite bodyplan origins or is a flightless neognath.
facts.quote: it is possible that Eremopezus represents a separate example of this, but it could equally be a flightless neognath of some kind.

facts.statement: Eremopezus may belong to a distinct family, Eremopezidae, because its closest relatives are unknown.
facts.quote: its placement in a distinct family Eremopezidae may well be warranted, as its closest relatives remain completely obscure.

facts.statement: If Eremopezus was a palaeognath, it is considered the most unusual one known to date.
facts.quote: if it was a palaeognath, it probably was the most unusual known to date

facts.statement: No known palaeognaths evolved gripping feet like Eremopezus, nor did they thrive in wetland habitats like those in the Jebel Qatrani Formation.
facts.quote: No palaeognaths are known to have evolved gripping feet like seen in the fossils, however, nor did they fare very successfully in wetland habitat as represented in the Jebel Qatrani Formation.

facts.statement: Eremopezus was a gigantic bird with well-known legs extending from the lower leg to the midfoot.
facts.quote: the legs (the lower leg to midfoot actually) of this gigantic bird are rather well-known today

facts.statement: Eremopezus possessed a tarsometatarsus with a small hypotarsus featuring a single simple crest and lacking foramina for tendons.
facts.quote: The tarsometatarsus had a small hypotarsus with a single simple crest and devoid of foramina for tendons.

facts.statement: A conspicuous ridge on the back of the Eremopezus tarsometatarsus was formed by the third toe's midfoot bones set to the plantar side and fused with neighbors.
facts.quote: The conspicuous ridge on the backside of the tarsometatarsus is formed by the third toe's midfoot bones, which are set to the plantar side in respect to their neighbors, with which they are fused.

facts.statement: The toes of Eremopezus differed significantly in shape and posture from those of rheas and most other birds.
facts.quote: Its toes, however, differed vastly in shape and posture from those of this ratite (and most other birds).

facts.statement: The third or middle toe of Eremopezus was the most robust and largest.
facts.quote: The third (middle) toe was the most robust and largest.

facts.statement: The hallux of Eremopezus was vestigial, though it may have been entirely missing as seen in ratites.
facts.quote: Its hallux was vestigial, as is typical for birds that move about on foot a lot; it even cannot be ruled out that the hallux was entirely missing (as in ratites).

facts.statement: Eremopezus eocaenus was somewhat ponderous and had a body size similar to Mullerornis betsilei.
facts.quote: E. eocaenus was somewhat ponderous, at about the body size of Mullerornis betsilei.

facts.statement: Eremopezus likely stood slightly less than one meter high from the ground to the pelvis, comparable to a large rhea or small emu.
facts.quote: From the ground to the pelvis, it stood probably as high as a large rhea or small emu—slightly less than one meter in all probability

facts.statement: Based on bone diameters of approximately 20mm, Eremopezus is estimated to have had a body mass between 25 and 30 kg.
facts.quote: The most complete tarsometatarsus and tibiotarsus known both have a minimum diameter of ~20mm in anteroposterior view, suggesting a body mass somewhere in the range of 25–30 kg.

facts.statement: Paleontologists consider it unlikely that Eremopezus could fly because its bones were as stout as those of certainly flightless birds.
facts.quote: Paleontologists do not consider this likely however, due to the stoutness of the bones, which in such a degree is only known from birds that were certainly flightless.

facts.statement: Eremopezus likely had white, black, or grey feathers containing eumelanin but little carotenoids and phaeomelanins, typical of higher waterbirds in similar habitats.
facts.quote: Perhaps most likely it had white, black or grey feathers with at least some eumelanin but little carotenoids and phaeomelanins, as usual among the "higher waterbirds" in general, and specifically those that inhabit similar habitat.

facts.statement: Piscivory or generalist predation are plausible diets for Eremopezus given its habitat, although many flightless birds are herbivorous or omnivorous.
facts.quote: piscivory or generalist predation seem plausible given the habitat, though many flightless birds are herbivorous to omnivorous.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Eremopezus possessed a hook or "nail" on its bill tip if it was a pelecaniform, and robust conclusions about its habits remain impossible without further fossil data.
facts.quote: Without further fossil data on Eremopezus, we cannot draw any robust conclusions about its habits.

facts.statement: Only one species, the enormous and presumably flightless Eremopezus eocaenus, is known from fossil remains.
facts.quote: Solo se conoce a partir de los restos fósiles de una sola especie, el enorme y presumiblemente no volador Eremopezus eocaenus.

facts.statement: Fossils were found in the Upper Eocene Jebel Qatrani Formation near the Qasr el Sagha escarpment, north of Lake Birket Qarun near Faiyum in Egypt.
facts.quote: Esto era encontrado en depósitos de la formación Jebel Qatrani del Eoceno superior alrededor de la escarpa de Qasr el Sagha, al norte del lago Birket Qarun cerca de Faiyum en Egipto.

facts.statement: The rocks containing fossils were deposited in the Priabonian stage, with the oldest dating to about 36 million years ago and the youngest to no less than 33 million years ago.
facts.quote: Las rocas en las que se encuentran sus fósiles se depositaron en el Priaboniano, y la más antigua data de hace unos 36 millones de años (Ma) y la más joven no menos de unos 33 Ma.

facts.statement: Fossils were previously thought to be from the Early Oligocene (33-30 Ma), but this is now considered incorrect.
facts.quote: Anteriormente se los consideraba de la edad del Oligoceno temprano, unos 33-30 Ma, pero ahora se supone que esto es incorrecto

facts.statement: The genus was described by Andrews in 1904.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Andrews, 1904

facts.statement: The species was described by Andrews in 1904.
facts.quote: species_authority: Andrews, 1904

facts.statement: The animal is classified in the infraclass Palaeognathae.
facts.quote: infraclassis: Palaeognathae

facts.statement: The animal belongs to the family Eremopezidae.
facts.quote: familia: †Eremopezidae

facts.statement: The time range is from the Priabonian to the Rupelian, between 37.71 and 27.3 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Priabonian to Rupelian (37.71 to 27.3 million years ago)

facts.statement: Fossils date from a time when the region had more forest and less grassland than it did six million years later.
facts.quote: The Eremopezus fossils dated with confidence are from a time when there was apparently more forest and less grassland in the region than half a dozen million years later.

facts.statement: The habitat likely resembled the modern Niger Delta.
facts.quote: Altogether, the habitat must have resembled the Niger Delta of our time.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that E. eocaenus might have been a frugivore or herbivore of swamp forests, though early Neoaves are generally predatory.
facts.quote: E. eocaenus might have been a frugivore or even herbivore of swamp forests, but the early Neoaves (to which it probably belonged) are generally predatory.

facts.statement: As a predator, it likely fed mainly on mid-sized terrestrial vertebrates such as large reptiles or small mammals.
facts.quote: As a predator, it would have fed mainly on mid-sized terrestrial vertebrates—for example large reptiles or smallish mammals.

facts.statement: Unmated birds were probably solitary.
facts.quote: Unmated birds were probably solitary.

facts.statement: It is debated whether flightless birds can compete with carnivorous mammals, as the Phorusrhacidae prove that carnivorous flightless birds can thrive alongside mammalian competitors.
facts.quote: It is sometimes believed that flightless birds cannot compete with carnivorous mammals, but the Phorusrhacidae prove that even carnivorous flightless birds can very well thrive in the presence of mammalian competitors.
